title: Insert interval
label: idb-list
statement: You have a list of closed intervals **sorted by start and not overlapping**. Insert one new interval, merging it with every interval it overlaps or touches, and return the new list — still sorted and non-overlapping.
provenance: **InterviewDB-listed.** LeetCode 57 is on the LinkedIn list you supplied from InterviewDB. No candidate report of this exact question was found in the research passes — the evidence is that the list names it. On that list it is a variation of InterviewDB Q9. The closest public problem to Q9. Identical merge-on-insert logic. The difference is what is returned: 57 rebuilds and returns the list in O(n); Q9 must keep a running covered total so the query is O(1) and the insert stays O(log n). LeetCode 715 Range Module (Hard) is the version that keeps state across calls.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: You have a list of closed intervals **sorted by start and not overlapping**. Insert one new interval, merging it with every interval it overlaps or touches, and return the new list — still sorted and non-overlapping.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Closed intervals — do [1,2] and [2,3] merge? (Yes.)
- Is the input guaranteed sorted and disjoint? (Yes — that is what makes one pass possible.)
- Return a new array or modify the input? (New array.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Because the list is sorted and disjoint, it splits into three runs: intervals entirely before the new one, intervals that overlap it, and intervals entirely after. Copy the first run, fold the middle run into one interval, copy the last run. One pass, O(n).

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "T."he sorted, disjoint input splits into three runs — before, overlapping, after — so one pass copies the first, folds the second into the new interval and copies the third: O(n)."

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works

learn.md:
**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Faster than O(n)?* — Binary-search where the overlap begins and ends — but building the output is still O(n) with an array.

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe the sorted, disjoint input splits into three runs — before, overlapping, after — so one pass copies the first, folds the second into the new interval and copies the third: O(n). Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Insert concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Appending and re-sorting the whole list — O(n log n) and throws away the given order.
- Using `<` instead of `<=` for the overlap test, so touching intervals do not merge.
- Forgetting the case where the new interval goes last.

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Many threads insert into a shared calendar.* — One lock around the whole insert, or copy-on-write: build the new list, swap a reference.

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *Millions of intervals, frequent inserts.* — A balanced tree keyed by start (SortedDictionary / SortedSet) makes each insert O(log n + merged) — InterviewDB Q9 is this structure.

learn.md:
**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *How would you test it?* — Brute force on a bitmap of small coordinates over random inputs.
